name: Touch to Reposition
target_behavior: Train clean entry, visible scoring, and immediate departure from the bad position. This is the core behavioral drill for teaching athletes not to stay in the exchange after success.
purpose: Train clean entry, visible scoring, and immediate departure from the bad position. This is the core behavioral drill for teaching athletes not to stay in the exchange after success.
standard_setup: Use open floor space or ring space. One feeder or partner presents a stable target or controlled live picture. Athlete starts in stance with enough room to enter, score, and leave on angle or line.
execution:
Athlete establishes stance and visual control before the rep begins.

Athlete enters under control behind feet and straight scoring logic.

Athlete lands the agreed scoring action or touch sequence.

Athlete immediately repositions to a better spot rather than admiring the work.

Athlete resets stance and eyes before the next rep.
what_good_looks_like:
Feet arrive before hands on entry, weight balanced, eyes already on target.
The scoring touch lands clean and visible from outside the opponent's direct line [A2-063].
The lead foot pivots off the centerline the instant contact is made, weight already transferring.
Stance and eye line are reset before the next call, with no pause standing in the pocket.
what_bad_looks_like:
Athlete stands square after the touch lands, watching the result.
Entry travels straight down the centerline instead of stepping off it.
Hands land before the base is set, feet trailing the punch.
Eyes reset late, after the feet have already moved, instead of before the next rep begins.
common_errors:
Staying too long after scoring.

Entering with hands before the base is under control.

Leaving straight back with poor balance when an angle is available.

Treating the drill like speed work instead of precision work.
corrections:
Coach calls "off" the instant the touch lands, before the athlete has time to admire it.
Coach physically blocks the straight retreat lane so the only open path is the lateral step.
Coach runs the entry footwork alone, no hands, until foot-before-hand order is automatic.
Coach freezes the rep on contact and places the athlete's feet by hand into the correct angle.
transfer:
Repetition of clean stance, entry, and touch under structured drilling produces measurable gains in stance and straight-punch execution within weeks [A2-068].
In live rounds this builds the habit of hit-and-move rather than hit-and-stay, and a visible off-line touch is scored where a square, admired one may be missed [A2-063].

name: Three and Out
target_behavior: Train exchange restraint, visible finish, and structural discipline. This drill teaches that the athlete does not need unlimited punches to own the exchange.
purpose: Train exchange restraint, visible finish, and structural discipline. This drill teaches that the athlete does not need unlimited punches to own the exchange.
standard_setup: Use pads, partner gloves, or controlled live partner work. Set a hard cap of three punches. The last punch is the structural finish and must be followed immediately by reposition.
execution:
Athlete enters with a declared scoring sequence.

Athlete throws no more than three punches.

The third shot finishes the scoring phase visibly.

Athlete exits immediately after the third punch.

Athlete resets before the next entry.
what_good_looks_like:
Athlete throws exactly three punches per entry, no more, before exiting range.
The third punch lands with full extension and visible weight transfer, closing the phase [A6-055].
Hands return to guard and feet reset before the next entry begins.
Punch selection varies entry to entry rather than repeating the same triple-punch pattern [A8-052].
what_bad_looks_like:
A fourth punch is thrown after the declared finish, extending past the drill's structure.
The third punch is flicked or arm-only, with no visible commitment to close the exchange.
Athlete remains planted in range after punch three instead of exiting.
The same three-punch sequence is repeated on every entry regardless of angle or opening.
common_errors:
Greed after success.

Poor awareness of sequence count.

Losing stance during the second or third punch.

Throwing the sequence too fast to control the finish.
corrections:
Coach calls "out" the instant a fourth punch starts and stops the rep immediately.
Coach has the athlete rerun the entry and calls for full extension and weight commitment specifically on punch three.
Coach steps into the athlete's forward path after punch three to force the exit step.
Coach names a new three-punch sequence before each entry so the athlete cannot default to a repeated pattern.
transfer:
Live exchanges lengthen in reaction time and lose punch force the longer they run [A3-032]; this drill builds the habit of committing to a clean finish early instead of drifting into extra output.
Outside the gym, the same discipline applies: state your point, make it clearly, and stop rather than overextending past the moment it lands.

name: Structured Pursuit
target_behavior: Train controlled pressure without chasing. This is a movement and decision drill, not a sprint drill.
purpose: Train controlled pressure without chasing. This is a movement and decision drill, not a sprint drill.
standard_setup: One partner or feeder gives ground under controlled conditions. Space should allow the athlete to cut, step, and own ground without having to rush. Use floor markers if needed.
execution:
Athlete advances behind stance, not behind emotional urgency.

Athlete uses step patterns and straight scoring threats to control space.

Athlete cuts and meets movement rather than simply following it.

Athlete scores only when the feet and picture are correct.

Athlete leaves the exchange correctly after scoring.
what_good_looks_like:
Feet arrive before the hands do; the jab or straight lands only after the back foot has replaced under the hip.
The pursuing athlete cuts the ring at an angle, meeting the retreating athlete's line rather than trailing it.
Scores come as single straight punches thrown from a set base, not from a moving base [A2-015].
After the punch lands, the scoring athlete replaces distance and resets stance before re-engaging.
what_bad_looks_like:
Feet cross or drag while advancing, so the punch is thrown while still moving forward.
Shoulders square up to the retreating partner instead of staying staggered behind the lead hand.
The athlete keeps advancing straight down the centerline instead of angling to cut off the ring.
After scoring, the athlete stays planted in range instead of exiting off-line.
common_errors:
Mistaking motion for pressure.

Trying to win the rep by speed instead of position.

Allowing frustration to shorten decision time.

Throwing while off the base.
corrections:
Stop the drill the moment the feet cross or the base collapses, and walk the step pattern in isolation before live pursuit resumes.
Call "angle" out loud on repetitions where the athlete follows a straight line, and have the pair repeat the exchange at a controlled pursuit speed until the cut-off angle appears on its own.
Restrict scoring credit to punches thrown from a stopped, replaced base — no credit for punches thrown mid-step — so the athlete self-corrects timing rather than being told about it.
Pair a structured walk-through-then-drill progression rather than open pursuit from the first rep; a structured teaching sequence produces cleaner technical pickup than unstructured repetition [B1-020], and short blocks of structured drilling have shown measurable stance and straight-punch improvement in a matter of weeks [A2-068].
transfer:
This is what keeps a boxer's range intact under real forward pressure in sparring — advancing on a plan instead of on adrenaline.
Outside the gym, it is the same discipline: closing on a goal deliberately, checking your footing at each step, rather than rushing the last few feet and losing your position.

name: Post Contact Reset
target_behavior: Train immediate recovery of structure after either giving or receiving contact. The athlete learns that contact is not a cue for emotional continuation.
purpose: Train immediate recovery of structure after either giving or receiving contact. The athlete learns that contact is not a cue for emotional continuation.
standard_setup: Use controlled partner touch, controlled sparring pictures, or pad interruptions. The coach should be able to trigger the reset repeatedly without needing full-intensity contact.
execution:
Athlete experiences the contact trigger.

Athlete does not answer emotionally.

Athlete resets stance, eyes, and breathing quickly.

Athlete resumes from structure, not from panic or momentum.
what_good_looks_like:
Feet return to base width and correct angle within one beat of the contact.
Eyes stay locked on the opponent, not on the glove or the point of impact.
One sharp exhale follows contact, then breathing settles into its normal rhythm.
Hands return to guard and weight centers before the next exchange begins.
what_bad_looks_like:
Athlete freezes upright with weight flat on both heels after contact.
Athlete chases, swings back, or retaliates before stance is reformed.
Athlete drops hands, turns the head away, or breaks eye contact with the opponent.
Athlete holds the breath or breathes rapidly and shallow through the mouth only.
common_errors:
Emotional retaliation.

Loss of visual control.

Breath holding.

Confusing speed with recovery.
corrections:
Coach calls "reset" as a fixed verbal cue the instant contact occurs.
Coach freezes the pair and checks foot placement, hand position, and eye line before allowing continuation.
Coach isolates the single contact-then-reset sequence, repeating it standing still before adding footwork or exchange back in.
Coach has the athlete exhale audibly on command until the sharp exhale becomes automatic after contact.
transfer:
This reset habit is what lets a boxer keep working behind increased ring movement and defensive movement, the pattern that now defines elite exchanges [A3-021][A2-064][A6-037].
Outside the gym, the same skill is catching a jolt, a setback, or a provocation without answering it emotionally, and resuming from a settled position instead of momentum or panic.

name: Chaos Recognition
target_behavior: Train the athlete to identify when the exchange is no longer worth staying in. The drill teaches leaving disorder instead of trying to solve it from inside the mess.
purpose: Train the athlete to identify when the exchange is no longer worth staying in. The drill teaches leaving disorder instead of trying to solve it from inside the mess.
standard_setup: Use controlled live partner work with deliberate disruptions: off-beat punches, crowding, awkward spacing, or broken rhythm. The coach must keep it educational, not random.
execution:
Athlete enters a live or semi-live exchange picture.

Partner creates controlled disorder.

Athlete identifies the breakdown point.

Athlete exits, repositions, and resets rather than trying to out-chaos the moment.
what_good_looks_like:
Athlete breaks contact and steps off the centerline before the second flurry lands.
Feet reset to fighting stance before hands reset to guard.
Athlete re-enters on a fresh angle, not the line the disorder occurred on.
Exchange picture resets clean, like the start of a new round rather than a continuation of the last one.
what_bad_looks_like:
Athlete stays inside range trying to trade shot for shot.
Athlete covers and absorbs instead of leaving.
Athlete backs straight up along the same line, still in range.
Athlete drops the guard the moment they disengage.
common_errors:
Late recognition.

Pride-driven staying.

Poor visual awareness under crowding.

Lack of agreement about what counts as disorder.
corrections:
Coach calls "out" the instant the exit should have happened and freezes the drill on that frame.
Coach walks the exit step by step at reduced speed before adding contact back in.
Coach narrows the disorder window so the exit decision has to come earlier and cleaner.
If the partner's disorder tips into unintended head contact, coach stops the drill immediately and follows the standard head-contact suspension protocol before any restart [B4-017].
transfer:
This is the same decision a boxer makes between rounds: the sport already builds in a hard reset rather than a continuation, which is why the one-minute interval exists [A6-022].
Outside the ring it is the same skill: recognizing when to leave a bad exchange or bad situation instead of trying to win it from inside.

name: Base Find and Freeze
execution: Step into stance from a walk on a call; hold 3s while the coach checks foot line, knee softness and weight distribution. Reset and repeat from a different walking direction.
what_good_looks_like:
Feet land staggered on the first step of the call, lead foot pointed at the target, rear foot turned out.
Knees show a soft bend, hips level, no lockout.
Weight sits centered between both feet, athlete can rock forward and back without losing balance.
Freeze holds still for the full count, no foot adjustment after landing.
what_bad_looks_like:
Feet land square and even, no stagger between lead and rear.
Knees locked straight, weight dropped back onto the heels.
Weight pooled on one foot, shoulders or hips leaning off center.
Feet shuffle or reset after landing to find balance instead of arriving set.
corrections:
Call the foot line out loud and point to where the lead foot should sit, have the athlete look down and check it themselves.
Tap the knee or hip to cue give, have the athlete bounce twice in place to feel the soft bend before freezing again.
Place a hand on the shoulder and press gently forward and back to test the base, name which foot is overloaded.
Send the athlete back to the walk start and call the freeze again from a new direction so the foot line has to be found fresh, not remembered.
transfer:
A base that holds without drifting is what lets footwork and ring movement work later, and movement volume becomes more important as the rule set has shifted toward it [A8-004].
Novice boxers lose work rate and structure late in a bout [A8-052], so a base that stays set under fatigue, not just on a fresh call, is the same skill this drill is building early.

name: Base Under Light Push
execution: Partner applies a slow two-hand push to the shoulders from varied directions; athlete absorbs without stepping. Push is slow and announced — this is a stability check, not a contest.
what_good_looks_like:
Feet stay planted through the full push, no step taken in any direction.
Knees stay soft and flex slightly on contact, absorbing force downward through the base.
Hips shift slightly opposite the push direction while shoulders stay square to the partner.
Athlete resets to original stance width and weight distribution immediately after the push releases.
what_bad_looks_like:
Athlete steps backward or sideways to catch balance.
Knees lock straight, so the push travels straight into the upper body and rocks the spine.
Athlete leans forward into the push instead of receiving it through the base.
Feet drift narrow or cross during the push, reducing the base under load.
corrections:
Coach slows the push further and announces direction out loud before contact.
Coach places a hand or foot marker at the athlete's current stance width and has them return to it after each push.
Coach cues "bend the knees" and taps the athlete's knee before the push lands.
Coach widens the drill stance manually, hands on hips, and repeats the same push until the base holds.
transfer:
This is the same base that has to hold when a real punch lands unexpectedly during exchanges, where hip and stance work is constant rather than occasional [A8-003].
Novices who drill stance this way show measurable stance improvement that holds up weeks later, not just in the same session [A2-068].

name: Line Walk to Base
execution: Walk a taped line, and on the call turn out into stance with feet either side of it. The tape gives an external reference for foot width and lead-foot angle.
what_good_looks_like:
Feet land on opposite sides of the tape the instant the call sounds.
Lead foot angles slightly inward toward the target, rear foot turned outward.
Weight settles evenly between both feet, knees soft, no lean forward or back.
Walking pace stays smooth and unbroken right up to the call.
what_bad_looks_like:
Both feet land on the same side of the line.
A foot steps directly on the tape instead of straddling it.
Lead foot points straight ahead or turns outward instead of angling in.
Athlete stutters, hops, or stalls the walk before turning out.
corrections:
Coach stands at the call point and taps the ground where each foot should land.
Slow the walking cadence so the turn-out lands on a clean count instead of a rush.
Lay a second strip of tape as a landing target for the rear foot.
Run the straddle without the call first, then add the call once the foot spacing is consistent.
transfer:
This straddle is the base every punch and defensive shift launches from, and footwork has taken on more weight in the sport as rule changes pushed boxers toward more ring movement and less standing exchange [A3-021][A8-004].
Outside the gym, the same habit - stop, feet apart, weight centered - is the ready position for any quick change of direction, on a field, a sidewalk, or a bus that starts moving.

name: Recovery Step Reset
execution: Coach calls a direction; athlete takes one committed step and recovers to base in a single movement. Score the recovery, not the step.
what_good_looks_like:
Feet land at shoulder width, base restored before the step foot fully settles.
Hands stay at guard height through the entire step-and-recover sequence.
Step and recovery happen as one motion, not step-then-adjust.
Eyes stay on the coach, not on the athlete's own feet.
what_bad_looks_like:
Overstepping past a recoverable distance, weight left on the front foot.
Crossing the feet or clipping the lead foot behind the rear foot.
Hands drop or drift down during the step, guard opens on recovery.
Two distinct movements visible — a step, then a separate scramble back to base.
corrections:
Call the same direction again immediately, no explanation, let the rep correct itself.
Shorten the called step distance until the single-motion pattern returns.
Tap the athlete's hands back to guard height without stopping the drill.
Freeze the athlete mid-recovery and physically square their feet to base.
transfer: This is the footwork underneath every exchange — displace, reset, stay available to punch or defend again. Rule changes in elite amateur boxing have pushed the sport toward more ring movement and more foot movement generally [A8-004], and a boxer who can't recover base after every step is late for whatever comes next, in the ring or moving through a crowd.

name: Off-Balance Recovery
execution: Partner gives a light directional nudge at random; athlete recovers base without crossing feet. Nudge intensity stays low and constant.
what_good_looks_like:
Feet reset to shoulder width without crossing or stepping wide.
Hands stay up at guard height through the entire recovery, not just after it [A2-060].
Weight settles back over the base foot before the next nudge arrives.
Head stays level, eyes on partner, no forward lean-in to catch balance.
what_bad_looks_like:
Feet cross during the recovery step.
Guard drops while the athlete focuses on footwork [A2-060].
Athlete overcorrects and steps well past a stable base, landing off-balance the other direction.
Recovery happens late, after the nudge has already displaced the hips, not during it.
corrections:
Stop the drill and reset feet by hand to the correct width when crossing occurs.
Call "hands" the instant the guard drops, independent of footwork quality.
Cue a shorter step and lower nudge intensity if overcorrection continues.
Slow the nudge cadence so the athlete recovers during the push, not after it.
transfer:
This base-recovery pattern is what shows up as the increased foot movement and defensive movement seen in modern ring performance [A3-021][A2-064].
Outside the gym, it is the same instinct that keeps someone upright on a crowded sidewalk or a moving train without a wild step to catch themselves.

name: Seated and Supported Base
target_behavior: Base definition for the adaptive lane
purpose: Base definition for the adaptive lane
execution: Base is defined with the athlete rather than prescribed: establish the most stable repeatable position available, whether seated, supported, or standing with an aid. Coach records the athlete's own base description for reuse.
what_good_looks_like:
Athlete settles into one position and holds it for the full drill without adjusting.
Base holds when weight shifts onto the lead or rear side.
Position matches the description the coach wrote down at the start.
Athlete returns to the same spot after moving the arms or trunk.
what_bad_looks_like:
Base changes between repetitions without being reset first.
Athlete leans past the edge of the support or grips the chair or frame for balance instead of resting on it as a base.
No written description of the base exists anywhere.
Base is copied from a standing athlete's stance rather than built from this athlete's own position.
corrections:
Coach stops the drill and has the athlete rebuild the position from stillness before continuing.
Coach writes the base down in plain terms - seated, supported, or standing with aid - and reads it back to the athlete for confirmation.
Coach repositions the chair, frame, or floor contact points until the base repeats without sliding.
Coach checks what is observed against the written description, not against a generic standing stance.
transfer:
A base the athlete can rebuild on command is what holds punch phases together once contact work is added [A6-055].
The written base description becomes the fixed reference point for every later session, recorded and checked rather than assumed [B2-008].

name: Supported Base Under Reach
execution: From the athlete's defined base, reach to targets at varying heights and return. The drill tests whether the base survives the reach, at whatever range the athlete owns.
what_good_looks_like:
Base stays planted through the full reach, no foot slide, no hop.
Hips and shoulders stay square to the target line as the arm extends.
Weight returns to the same base position after every reach.
Reach and return happen at the athlete's own working range without losing a support point.
what_bad_looks_like:
Base collapses or shifts at the top of the reach.
Trunk leans to close distance instead of the arm extending.
Support point - foot, chair edge, wheel, cane - lifts or slides under load.
Return to base is skipped or rushed, athlete stays extended past the reach.
corrections:
Shorten the target distance until the base holds through the entire reach.
Call "reach - and home" out loud on every rep to rebuild the return phase.
Set a hand or a marker at the support point so any drift is visible the instant it happens.
Slow the tempo and split the drill into two counted phases: reach, then return.
transfer:
A base that survives a reach is a base that survives a punch thrown at range - same structural test, different intent.
Structured base work of this kind has shown measurable improvement and retention over time [A2-068], so this drill is built to be repeated across sessions, not run once and checked off.

name: Weight Shift Metronome
execution: Shift weight lead-to-rear on a steady count without lifting either foot. Adds a rhythm reference before any punch is attached.
what_good_looks_like:
Weight rolls smoothly from lead foot to rear foot and back on the count, both feet staying flat on the floor.
Hips and shoulders shift together with the weight, not ahead of it or lagging behind it.
Head stays level and stacked over the base through each shift, no bobbing up or down.
Pressure builds into the forefoot on the loaded side in step with the shift, matching the pattern seen when punch acceleration and forefoot loading rise together [A2-008].
what_bad_looks_like:
Foot lifts, heel pops up, or foot rolls onto its edge during the shift.
Weight shift and upper body rotation land at different times instead of arriving together.
Athlete bounces vertically in place instead of shifting horizontally.
Shift is uneven across the count, quick one direction and dragging the other.
corrections:
Coach places a hand on the athlete's hip and calls the count aloud, timing hand pressure to the beat.
Coach freezes the athlete mid-shift and checks both feet are flat before resuming.
Coach strips the count down to hips-only movement until the transfer smooths out, then adds the full shift back in.
Coach stands in front of the athlete and mirrors the shift with his own body so the athlete matches tempo to a visible model.
transfer:
This is the same weight transfer that drives punch force once punches are attached, and impact force in boxers correlates with this kind of lower-body drive and its muscle activation pattern [A2-015].
Outside the gym, the same rhythmic control under a shifting load applies to lifting, changing direction, and any task where force is generated through the feet.

name: Transfer Into Empty Space
execution: Execute the transfer that would drive a rear-hand punch, but stop the hand at the shoulder. Isolates the legs from the arm so the sequence is felt rather than masked.
what_good_looks_like:
Rear foot pivots and hip rotates before the shoulder turns.
Weight shifts from the rear leg to the lead leg as the shoulder comes through.
Hand rises to shoulder height and stops - no extension, no fist rotation.
The sequence reads foot, hip, torso, shoulder, stop, in that order [A6-055].
what_bad_looks_like:
Shoulder or hand moves before the rear foot pivots.
Hand travels past shoulder height into extension.
Weight stays parked on the rear leg through the whole motion.
Torso rotates while the rear foot stays flat, disconnecting the hip from the upper body.
corrections:
Stop the rep the moment the hand outruns the hip.
Have the athlete run the pivot with hands on hips, no arm, until foot-hip-torso order is clean.
Place a hand on the athlete's rear hip to mark the pivot and set tempo.
Slow the whole motion down and count it aloud: foot, hip, shoulder, stop.
transfer:
This is the sequencing that produces force once a target is added - impact depends on momentum passed through the arm from the hips and legs, not arm strength alone [A2-003][A2-015].
That transfer habit has to hold up under fatigue, since both reaction time and punch force shift as sparring load builds [A8-029].

name: Loaded Transfer Hold
execution: Band anchored at hip height; complete the weight transfer against the band and hold the end position 2s. Band tension is light — this is a positional drill, not strength work.
what_good_looks_like:
Weight shifts fully onto the front foot as the punch extends, with hip rotation visibly leading the shoulder and the shoulder leading the fist [A6-055].
The band stays under light, even tension throughout — no slack, no jerk.
The end position holds still for the full 2 seconds: no foot shuffle, no rebalancing step, no arm dropping.
Transfer and hold look like one continuous motion, not "punch, then freeze."
what_bad_looks_like:
Weight stays on the back foot while only the arm reaches forward.
Shoulder or fist arrives before the hip has rotated — sequence is reversed.
Band pulls the athlete off their line, and they step or lean to catch balance during the hold.
Punch collapses at end range — elbow drops or torso folds instead of holding tall.
corrections:
Stand behind the athlete and place a hand on the hip to cue "hip starts it" before the fist moves.
Slow the rep down — have them pause at mid-transfer and name where their weight is.
Shorten the band's working range so the stability demand matches what they can currently hold clean.
Reset foot position between reps if the hold keeps drifting off-line; don't let a bad base repeat.
transfer:
This sequencing — hip before shoulder before fist, weight arriving fully forward — is the same loading pattern behind the highest recorded punch impact forces in boxers [A2-015].
Holding the end position under resistance builds the base needed to stay on balance when contact or a bad angle tries to pull it away.

name: Guard Set and Hold
execution: Set guard from hands-down on a call and hold while the coach checks elbow position, hand height and shoulder line. Reset between reps.
what_good_looks_like:
Hands sit at cheekbone height before the call, elbows tucked in front of the ribs, chin tucked behind the front shoulder.
Guard forms in one motion on the call, no separate movement of lead and rear hand.
Shoulders stay square to the coach, weight even on both feet.
Hands hold their height and elbow line without drift while the coach checks the position.
what_bad_looks_like:
Hands float above the head or drop below the cheekbone during the hold.
Elbows wing out away from the ribs, opening the body line.
Chin lifts or turns away from the front shoulder.
Rear hand rebuilds slower than lead hand, or one side collapses first under fatigue.
corrections:
Call "set" again and rebuild the guard from hands-down rather than nudging the existing position.
Tap the elbow that has flared and give it a fixed touch point to return to.
Place a hand under the chin as a physical reference until the tuck holds on its own.
Slow the call-and-hold tempo so both hands arrive and lock at the same time.
transfer:
A guard that holds its shape under a static check is the guard that stays up when fatigue and pressure start pulling it apart in sparring, and guard-drop time under fatigue has been recorded as a marker separating winners from losers in competition [A2-060].
The same discipline of returning to a fixed, checked position applies to posture and readiness in any task performed under repeated physical load outside the gym.

name: Guard Through Fatigue
execution: Hold guard through repeated short work bouts. The coach records the point at which hand height first drops — that timestamp is the useful output, not the total duration.
what_good_looks_like:
Hands sit at cheekbone height and stay there across every bout, not just the first one.
Elbows stay tucked to the ribs, chin stays down, centerline stays covered.
The athlete returns to guard in the same motion as the last movement, no gap between output and reset.
what_bad_looks_like:
Hand height drops as bout count rises — the same fatigue that drives sharp increases in blood lactate and cortisol during boxing-specific work shows up first in the hands [A5-006].
Elbows wing outward and the centerline opens.
Guard return lags behind footwork or output, arriving a beat late instead of automatic.

purpose: Using range as the primary defence

Athlete's rear foot and hip shift back just far enough that the partner's fingertips fall short by an inch or two.
Weight resettles evenly over both feet the instant the reach is avoided, no pause before the next action.
Hands stay at guard height and eyes stay on the partner's shoulder line through the whole movement.
The retreat distance is visibly the same size as the reach - no extra step tacked on.

Athlete takes two or three steps back when the reach only required one.
Athlete bends or leans from the waist instead of moving the feet.
Athlete drops the hands or turns the head away while retreating.
Athlete stands flat-footed until the reach is already close, then lunges backward to escape it.

Coach places a cone or line at the minimum safe distance and has the athlete retreat only to that mark.
Coach calls "feet" the instant a lean substitutes for a step, and restarts the rep.
Coach reduces the partner's reach speed until the athlete's retreat distance stays consistent, then rebuilds speed.
Coach counts steps out loud during the rep so the athlete hears when a second step is unnecessary.

Coach withholds authorization to escalate contact until the return is consistent at the current count.

Athlete answers each incoming punch with a different tool: slip, roll, parry, pivot, or step-off, never repeating the same response twice in a row.

Return to a stable guard position between each exchange, hands up, chin down, weight balanced.

Feet stay planted while only the upper body reacts, leaving the athlete square to follow-up punches.

Recovery after a defensive action is slow, leaving a flat-footed pause before the guard resets.

Stop the round and name the punch just thrown and the defense that should have answered it, then restart from that exact exchange.
Restrict the partner to a single punch type until the athlete shows the full range of defenses against it, then expand.
Slow the feed to isolate footwork from head movement, requiring a step or pivot before allowing any upper-body defense.

name: Broken Rhythm
execution: Alternate fast and delayed sequences on the coach's call. Rhythm change is the skill, not speed.
what_good_looks_like:
Fast combination snaps off on the call, then the next sequence sits half a beat longer before releasing.
Feet and hands change tempo together, not hands alone.

Every sequence lands at the same tempo regardless of the call - the coach's signal is being ignored.

Boxer speeds up the delayed call to catch up, erasing the gap that was supposed to be there.

Stop the round and call the two tempos back to back, isolated, until the contrast is clean before adding combinations.
Put a hand on the boxer's lead shoulder during the delay to check weight is still live, not parked.
Cut combination length and drill the rhythm break on a single shot pair until the gap is real and repeatable.

name: Punch From the New Angle
execution: Cut an angle, then punch from the position gained. A punch thrown before the angle is complete does not count.
what_good_looks_like:
Feet move first, plant on the new line, and only then does the hand fire [A8-004].
Weight drives through the rear leg into the punch rather than sitting in the shoulder [A3-030].
The punch lands on a line the opponent had not covered.
Angle and punch happen as one continuous action, not two separate beats.

Punch fired mid-step, before the foot plants on the new line.
Boxer cuts the angle, then squares back up before throwing.
Punch thrown from the arm alone, with no rear-leg drive behind it [A3-030].
Same angle cut on every repetition, so the pattern becomes predictable [A2-052].

Stop the rep and have the boxer walk the step alone, with no punch, until the foot plant is clean.

Change the called angle every few reps so the boxer cannot rely on repetition [A2-052].

name: Feint and Read

purpose: Producing a reaction with a feint

what_good_looks_like:
Feinting hand or shoulder starts the same initiation phase as a real punch, then halts before the strike phase begins [A8-007].
Partner's weight shifts onto the back foot, guard lifts, or eyes drop within a beat of the feint.
No real punch follows immediately - there is a visible pause between the feint and any further action.
Feinter names the specific reaction out loud right after it happens: which hand moved, which foot loaded, where the eyes went.

The feint runs past initiation into the strike phase and becomes an actual punch [A8-007].

Feinter reports a reaction that did not actually occur, guessed instead of observed.

Stop the drill the instant the feint extends past the initiation phase and reset to the start position [A8-007].
Ask directly: "what did his hand do, what did his foot do, where did his eyes go" until the answer is specific.

Partners start moving before the contract is spoken.
One partner raises intensity without a new spoken agreement.
Stop signal is given but the other partner works one more exchange before stopping.
Leader role is contested or unclear once the drill is underway.

Coach stops the pair on the spot and resets both to standing still, hands down.
Coach has both partners restate the contract out loud before any resumption.

name: Constraint Swap
target_behavior: Adapting when the task constraint changes
purpose: Adapting when the task constraint changes
execution: Run a known drill, then change one constraint — range, hand availability, footwork restriction — and run it again. The adaptation is the target, not the original drill.
what_good_looks_like:
Athlete runs the original drill clean before the constraint lands.
On the swap, footwork and hand selection change within the first two exchanges, not gradually.
Movement increases to cover what was taken away — more lateral steps, more ring generalship when range gets cut, more head movement when a hand is removed [A2-064].
Guard and stance hold through the transition, no reset or pause between the two drills.
what_bad_looks_like:
Athlete keeps running the original pattern after the constraint has changed.
Visible pause or verbal check before adjusting — decision lag you can see.
Restricted hand creeps back into use, or the cut range gets crossed once pressure rises.
Output just collapses instead of shifting — punch volume drops with no rise in movement or feints to cover the gap [A8-004].
corrections:
Stop the moment the old pattern reappears, name the constraint out loud, restart immediately.
Shrink the space or add a visual cue if the athlete can't find the adjustment on their own.
If the swap keeps getting missed as the round goes, cut the work segment short rather than let fatigue mask itself as poor adaptation — reaction time lengthens well before the athlete reports feeling slow [A8-029].
Walk the transition once at half speed, then send it back to full speed.

Fights change shape mid-round without warning — a hand goes dead, the ring shrinks, the opponent takes your range away. This drill is the rehearsal for that exact moment.
Outside the gym it's the same skill under a different name: the plan changes, you adjust the response, and you keep your frame while you do it.

name: Conditioned Sparring — Single Task

Attacker throws only the named action and nothing else, repetition after repetition.
Defender uses guard, slip, or pivot only, no return punches, no counters.
Attacker's off hand stays up and set between reps.
Both boxers reset to stance and hands-up before the next rep starts.
what_bad_looks_like:
Attacker adds a second punch or combination not named for the drill.
Defender fires back instead of defending only.
Pace or power creeps up past a controlled, no-contact standard.
Coach is not standing at the pairing, watching the exchange directly.
corrections:
Stop the pair on the first mixed-in punch or returned shot, name the single action again out loud, restart from stance.
Walk the pair through the action at half speed before letting them go back to drill pace.
Pull a pair that keeps breaking the restriction out of sparring and put them on solo shadow work instead.

One clean, accurate shot beats a wide, busy attack — this is what separates winners from losers in the amateur scoring data, not punch volume [A8-002].

name: Open Sparring

Coach stops the session on sight of any head-blow stoppage criteria and does not resume without ringside medical input [B4-017].

name: Sparring Debrief

what_good_looks_like:
Athlete and coach each state one thing that worked and one that did not, in that order, before either hears the other's version.
Statements name a specific action — a round number, a punch, a position — not a general impression.
The two lists are compared out loud within minutes of the sparring ending, gear still on.
Where the two lists disagree, both parties say so and point to the exchange in question.
what_bad_looks_like:
Athlete waits to hear the coach's note before giving their own.
The note is vague — "I did alright," "my jab was off" — with no round or exchange attached.
The debrief turns into a full replay of the sparring session instead of two points.
The comparison gets pushed to the next day instead of happening right after the bout.
corrections:
Coach has both parties write their one-good/one-bad note down before either speaks, so the second person can't just echo the first.

When an answer is vague, coach asks "what round, what happened" and does not accept a second vague answer.
When the athlete drifts into replaying the whole sparring session, coach stops them and repeats: one thing that worked, one that did not.

The athlete carries one specific correction into the next sparring session instead of a general mood about how it went.
The habit of separating what happened from how it felt is useful in any review of performance, in or out of the gym.

name: Stop Signal Rehearsal
execution: Partners rehearse the stop signal cold, before any contact work, until the response is immediate. Rehearsed before every contact session regardless of athlete experience.
what_good_looks_like:
Both partners run the signal cold, before any gloves touch, and the response comes on the first call, not the second.
Signal given — hand up or word called — receiver's hands drop and both athletes step back inside the same second.
Eye contact is made and the receiver waits for a spoken "ready" before either partner resumes.
Called twice in a row, the response stays just as fast the second time.
what_bad_looks_like:
Receiver keeps punching, moving, or finishing a combination after the signal is given.
Signal-giver hesitates, mumbles the call, or skips it out of embarrassment.
Pair races through the rehearsal once and treats it as done rather than testing it to failure.
Athlete nods or gestures instead of using the trained signal.

Stop the drill outright and reset both athletes to neutral before any contact work is allowed to start or continue.
Call the signal yourself, time the response, and work pair by pair — supervision, not floor space, is what limits how many pairs you can watch in this kind of technical drilling [B2-046].
Have the athlete who hesitated call the signal five times cold, alone, before putting them back with a partner.

The habit of calling a stop early, before pushing through, carries the same way outside the gym: say something before it escalates, not after.

name: Intensity Cap Check
execution: Partners agree an intensity level, work briefly, then each rate the actual intensity. Mismatched ratings mean the cap is not shared and the pairing needs coach attention.
what_good_looks_like:
Both partners state the same intensity number out loud to each other and to the coach before starting.
The work stays brief, hands and feet stay technical, shots land with control rather than power.
The moment work stops, each partner rates the actual intensity independently, before either speaks to the other.
The two ratings match or sit one number apart.
what_bad_looks_like:
One partner calls the exchange "70 percent" while the other calls the same exchange "90 percent."
Intensity climbs round to round without either partner naming the change, work getting sharper as the drill continues [A3-024].
A partner gives their rating only after hearing the other's number, not before.
A partner nods at the agreed cap but cannot repeat it back in their own words.
corrections:
Stop the pairing the instant ratings diverge and have each partner reproduce the intensity they meant, side by side, for comparison.
Have each partner call their number facing away from the other, before any discussion, every single time.
Before work starts, make each partner restate the agreed cap in their own words rather than just agreeing to it [A8-035].
Shorten the work interval so the check happens more often, catching drift before it builds across rounds [A3-024].

The habit of naming a cap, checking it, and stopping on mismatch is what holds a boundary once heart rate and fatigue climb in live sparring [A3-024].

name: Between-Round Reset

Athlete returns to the stool or corner and takes several full breaths before any instruction is given.
Coach delivers exactly one instruction, stated once, in plain language.

Athlete is still breathing hard through the mouth when the bell sounds, no visible settling of breath.
Athlete stands or shifts weight onto the back foot instead of resetting to base stance.
Coach and athlete go back and forth talking instead of one instruction landing and stopping.
corrections:
Coach stops after the first instruction and physically holds up one finger as the cap.
Coach calls "breathe" and pauses three seconds before saying anything else.
Coach places hands on athlete's shoulders or taps the guard position to force the return to base stance.
Coach shortens the instruction to a single cue word if the athlete cannot execute a full sentence in time.

name: Instruction Under Fatigue

Coach gives one instruction between bouts, athlete applies it on the first exchange of the next bout.

Athlete pauses for a beat before responding, instruction is being processed rather than acted on [B4-015].
Athlete asks the coach to repeat the instruction mid-bout.

Cut the instruction down to one word or one image, not a sentence, before the next bout starts.
Demonstrate the correction on the pads in the seconds before the bout starts rather than describing it.
Watch only the first exchange of the next bout - if the correction isn't there, stop the bout and reset with the identical cue.
Drop the pace of the next work bout so the instruction can be executed clean before fatigue is reintroduced.

This is the exact demand of a corner instruction between rounds - one cue, delivered once, executed cold on the first exchange of the next round.

name: Lead Foot Battle
target_behavior: Managing lead-foot position against opposite stance
purpose: Managing lead-foot position against opposite stance
execution: Against an opposite-stance partner, work to keep the lead foot outside theirs. No punching.
what_good_looks_like:
Lead foot lands outside the partner's lead foot on every reset, opening the angle toward their back hip.
Weight returns to stance cleanly, no crossing of the feet during the reposition.
The foot adjusts on the partner's step, not after their hips have already turned.
Stance stagger stays intact through the exchange; shoulders stay offset, not squared.
what_bad_looks_like:
Lead foot drifts inside the partner's lead foot, giving up the outside angle.
Feet cross during the repositioning step.
The response to the partner's step arrives late, after the hips have already turned.
Athlete squares up, stance stagger disappears.
corrections:
Coach calls "outside" the moment the angle is lost, freezes both athletes, and resets from that exact foot position.
Coach slows the rep to half speed and repeats the same step until the crossing stops showing up.
Coach has the partner step first and restricts the athlete to a lead-foot pivot only, isolating the correction from everything else.
Coach closes the working space when squaring recurs, forcing a smaller, quicker outside step.
transfer:
Holding this angle deep into a bout is a conditioning problem as much as a technical one; aerobic capacity is what lets the footwork stay disciplined instead of breaking down under fatigue [A5-002][A3-022].
Winners in novice bouts throw more lead-hand punches in round one than losers [A2-059]; lead-foot position is what makes that lead hand land, so the habit built here shows up first in early-round scoring.

name: Plan and Adjust
target_behavior: Changing plan when it is not working
purpose: Changing plan when it is not working
execution: Athlete states a plan, works a bout, then states what they changed and why. Requires coach authorization.
what_good_looks_like:
Athlete states the plan in one sentence before the round starts — stance, target, footwork.
When the opponent switches stance, the athlete's lead foot and guard hand swap within the next two exchanges.
Coach gives a visible go/no-go signal before the athlete resumes after any pause to adjust.
After the bout, athlete points to the exact exchange where the plan stopped working and names what replaced it.
what_bad_looks_like:
Athlete keeps running the original plan for rounds after the stance switch has changed the angles.
Lead foot and jab hand stay fixed even though the opponent's lead hand has changed.
Athlete describes the outcome ("I got caught") instead of naming what in the plan needs to change.
Athlete changes the plan mid-round without waiting for coach authorization.
corrections:
Coach stops the round and has the athlete call out the opponent's current stance before anything else.
Coach walks the athlete through the footwork swap standing still, then restarts from that position.
Coach withholds authorization to continue until the athlete states the revised plan in one sentence.
Coach flags the point in the bout where the athlete's reads got slow, since reaction speed and decision measures in boxers decline across bout load within a tournament [B4-015].
transfer:
Naming what changed and switching the response before frustration builds carries directly into live sparring and into competition against an unfamiliar stance.
The habit of stating a plan, testing it, and revising it out loud is the same habit that solves problems outside the gym.

name: Opponent Problem Solving
execution: Coach assigns the partner a specific behaviour; athlete must identify and address it. Requires coach authorization.
what_good_looks_like:
Athlete's shot selection changes visibly between rounds in direct response to the assigned behavior.
Range, angle, and rhythm shift round to round instead of repeating the same entry against the same cue [A2-061].
Punch accuracy against the specific behavior improves as the rounds continue rather than staying flat [A2-061].
Defensive movement rises specifically against the imposed behavior, not as a general increase in busyness.
what_bad_looks_like:
Athlete throws the same combination that already failed, unchanged, in a later round.
Athlete only reacts to the behavior after being caught by it repeatedly, not before.
Athlete drops the tactical assignment mid-round and reverts to a default, comfortable pattern.
Athlete makes random adjustments instead of ones tied to the specific cue the coach assigned.
corrections:
Coach stops the round immediately and states the exact behavior the athlete failed to solve.
Coach isolates one cue-response pairing on the pads or in shadow work before sending the pair back in.
Coach, holding current certification and authorization to run this drill, resets the partner to the assigned behavior and restarts the round [B3-045][A3-017].
Coach positions within direct sightline of every exchange so the adjustment can be scored live, not reconstructed after [B2-008].
transfer:
Carries straight into live sparring and bouts, where the opponent changes shape and the boxer has no timeout to think it over.
Carries into any pressure situation outside the gym where the first answer fails and a second, better-read answer is required on the spot.

name: Wrap Under Supervision
execution: Athlete wraps their own hands and a coach checks coverage and tightness before any bag or contact work. Wrap length and specification follow the applicable sanctioning body — there is no universal standard.
what_good_looks_like:
Athlete lays gauze and tape flat across the back of the hand with no twists or bunching.
Knuckles, thumb, and wrist are covered per the wrap specification named for that commission or gym. [A6-066]
Fist closes fully and fingers spread open with the wrap already in place, before gloves go on.
Coach checks tightness with a finger slid under the wrap at the wrist and gives a visible nod or thumbs-up before any bag contact.
what_bad_looks_like:
Wrap crosses the wrist bone directly instead of routing around it.
Tape touches bare skin instead of gauze, or tape substitutes for gauze across the knuckles.
Wrap is left loose over the knuckle line, or cinched so tight the fingers change color or the athlete cannot make a full fist.
Athlete moves to bag work before the coach has checked the wrap.
corrections:
Stop the athlete before gloving up and unwrap the section that is wrong.
Rewrap the wrist and knuckle area yourself once, narrating each pass, then hand control back to the athlete for the next hand.
Recheck fist closure and finger color after any tightness adjustment.
Hold the athlete at wrap-check stage — no bag, no mitts, no partner work — until coverage and tightness both pass. This matters because the hand is the single most frequently injured site in boxing, in training and in competition alike. [A2-070][A6-001][A6-009]
transfer:
Checking equipment before contact, and stopping when something is off, is the same habit that governs mouthguard checks, glove checks, and partner-readiness checks later in training.
Outside the gym it is the same discipline as checking gear before any task where a hand or tool failure only shows up after the fact.

name: General Movement Warm-Up
execution: Progressive whole-body movement building from walking to boxing-specific footwork over several minutes.
what_good_looks_like:
Boxer starts at a walk and the pace visibly climbs in stages, not in one jump.
Arm swings, hip rotation, and ankle bounce all show full range before any fast footwork appears.
By the final minutes the feet are already in boxing stance, weight shifting side to side in short steps.
Breathing stays controlled through the whole progression; no one is doubled over at the end.
what_bad_looks_like:
Boxer goes straight from standing to sprint-paced shuttles, skipping the walking and jogging stages.
Static stretches held for long counts appear before any pulse-raising movement.
Footwork copied from the coach looks flat-footed and square, with no stance narrowing as pace builds.
Group pace is uneven — some boxers coasting, others already sweating heavily before the drill's midpoint.
corrections:
Coach calls the group back to walking pace and restarts the progression from the top.
Coach removes any held static stretch from the front of the warm-up and moves it to the end if used at all.
Coach walks the floor calling "on your toes" and demonstrates the stance narrowing personally, boxer by boxer.
Coach splits fast starters from slow starters and sets a shared count so the whole group changes gear together.
transfer:
The staged build from walking to boxing footwork is the same shape a boxer's body goes through before rounds and sparring later in a session, matching how a full boxing session is structured around a warm-up phase before drill and conditioning work begins [B1-062].
Outside the gym, this is the same habit of raising pace gradually before any hard physical task — moving stiff joints and slow feet before asking them for speed.

name: Shoulder Preparation
target_behavior: Preparing the shoulder for punching volume
purpose: Preparing the shoulder for punching volume
execution: Controlled shoulder range work through the positions punching demands, before any bag or pad work.
what_good_looks_like:
Shoulders trace the full punching arc — jab line, hook rotation, uppercut drive — before any bag or pad contact begins.
Movement stays slow and controlled, never thrown or bounced.
Range builds progressively, from small circles into full extension.
Left and right shoulders move through matching range and matching reps.
what_bad_looks_like:
Rolls stop at a comfortable half-range and never reach full punching extension.
Motion is jerked or swung rather than driven under control.
One shoulder gets visibly less range than the other.
Athlete substitutes long static holds for the dynamic set, leaving the shoulder loose but not moved through the punching lines [A5-033].
corrections:
Coach halts the set and resets to half-speed reps until the motion is smooth and controlled.
Coach performs the range alongside the athlete so both sides can be matched visually.
Coach adds an end-range pause on the weaker side until it mirrors the stronger side.
Coach removes static stretching from this slot and keeps the set purely dynamic and punch-specific [A5-033].
transfer:
Full shoulder range here becomes jab and hook extension under load once punching volume climbs in sparring and rounds [A3-019].
A shoulder that has already cycled through the punching arc is the one that holds its form when work gets fast and repetitive.

name: Hip and Ankle Preparation
target_behavior: Preparing the lower body for stance and pivots
purpose: Preparing the lower body for stance and pivots
execution: Ankle and hip range work targeting the positions the boxing stance and pivot require.
what_good_looks_like:
Ankle reaches full dorsiflexion with heel staying grounded until the pivot calls for it.
Hip rotates through the joint, not the low back, with the pelvis and shoulders turning together.
Weight shifts smoothly from rear foot to lead foot without a hitch or double-step.
Knee tracks in line with the toes through the full range of the movement.
what_bad_looks_like:
Ankle stays flat and stiff, boxer pivots off a locked joint instead of rolling through it.
Knee caves inward as hip rotates, changing the line of the stance.
Rotation comes from twisting the low back while the hips stay square.
Reps rushed through a shortened range, missing the end position entirely.
corrections:
Slow the rep down and hold the end range for a full count before releasing.
Hands-on cue at the knee to reset tracking over the toes.
Reduce the range being asked for, rebuild it in small steps before adding more.
Demonstrate the pivot again side-on so the boxer sees hip and shoulder turning as one unit.
transfer:
This range and control is what lets the stance hold and the pivot fire cleanly once punches and footwork are added.
The same hip-and-ankle control shows up anywhere a person needs to change direction quickly without losing balance.

name: Neck Preparation
execution: Gentle controlled neck movement through range. This is preparation for training demand — it is not presented as concussion protection, for which the evidence does not support such a claim.
what_good_looks_like:
Head moves slowly through flexion, extension, and both lateral tilts with the chin leading each turn.
Shoulders stay level and still while the neck does the work.
Breathing stays even and unbroken through the full set.
Range increases gradually across repetitions rather than staying fixed or shrinking.
what_bad_looks_like:
Head snaps or bounces at the end of range instead of arriving there under control.
Shoulders rise or rotate to help generate the movement.
Boxer holds breath or braces the jaw during the motion.
Range shortens over the set, stopping short of full flexion or extension.
corrections:
Cue "slow it down" and have the boxer restart at half speed.
Place a hand on the boxer's shoulder to hold it down and give a fixed reference point.
Tell the boxer to breathe out through each turn, audibly if needed.
Cut the range back to what can be done under control, then rebuild it rep by rep.
transfer: Neck strength and controlled range work of this kind has shown general training effect in both untrained and trained populations [A5-106], and this drill is the entry point for that kind of loading, not a concussion safeguard — the research on neck strength and concussion risk shows no consistent protective link [A5-098]. What carries forward is a boxer who can hold head position steady under fatigue late in a round, which matters for defense and for everyday posture control outside the gym.

name: Cervical Endurance Hold
execution: Isometric holds in multiple directions. Trains neck endurance for training tolerance; no claim is made regarding head-injury risk.
what_good_looks_like:
Chin stays tucked and spine stays neutral through the entire hold.
Head holds a fixed position against resistance in each direction — flexion, extension, both lateral sides — without drift.
Breathing stays steady and rhythmic, no breath-holding.
Transition from one direction to the next is smooth, with no wobble or reset needed. Isometric holds of this kind are a standard, effective method for building neck muscular endurance [A5-106].
what_bad_looks_like:
Chin pokes forward or juts out to compensate for fatigue.
Shoulders shrug upward to assist the neck instead of the neck bearing the load alone.
Head visibly shakes or oscillates rather than holding a fixed point.
One direction (commonly lateral) is noticeably weaker, with the hold breaking down early only on that side.
corrections:
Cue "chin down, ears over shoulders" and physically tap the point of correct alignment.
Drop the resistance or hand pressure and rebuild the hold from a clean starting position.
Call out a breathing count so the athlete exhales through the hold instead of bracing and holding breath.
Isolate the weak direction and repeat it alone before returning to the full rotation.
transfer:
A neck that holds position under load stays that way when the head is jostled in a clinch or exchange, keeping the chin tucked by habit rather than by conscious effort.
This is a strength and endurance carryover only — it is not a claim that the drill lowers head-injury risk, and boxing's injury pattern still shows the head and neck concentrated in competition rather than training [B3-022].

name: Thoracic Rotation
execution: Controlled rotation through the thoracic spine, which the punching action requires.
what_good_looks_like:
Hips and feet stay fixed while the shoulders and rib cage rotate.
Rotation initiates from the mid-back, not the low back or neck.
Head trails the turn instead of leading it.
The trunk returns to center under control, with no bounce at end range.
what_bad_looks_like:
Pelvis or lower back rotates along with the shoulders.
Head snaps ahead of the spine to fake extra range.
Shoulders climb toward the ears during the turn.
Athlete bounces or jerks at the end of the range to force more rotation.
corrections:
Hands on the athlete's hips, cue "hips stay, ribs turn."
Run the drill seated to remove hip and leg compensation.
Shrink the range and rebuild it from a smaller, cleaner arc.
Cue shoulders down and away from the ears before each rep.
Expect the rate of improvement to differ by age and training background rather than follow one timeline for everyone [A5-033].
transfer:
This separation of hips from shoulders is the same mechanism that lets punching output travel through the trunk into the fist without dragging the low back along for the ride.
Outside the gym, it's the range that lets someone turn to check a blind spot or twist to reach behind a car seat without strain.

name: Cool-Down Walk and Breathe
execution: Low-intensity movement with extended exhalation until breathing settles.
what_good_looks_like:
Shoulders drop and stride shortens within the first minute of movement.
Exhale runs visibly longer than the inhale on every breath cycle.
Breathing rate slows and becomes even before the athlete stops moving.
Athlete stays upright and walking, not static and not seated.
what_bad_looks_like:
Athlete stops walking and stands frozen in place.
Breathing stays short and shallow with no extended exhale.
Athlete bends forward at the waist, hands on knees, head down.
Collapse, gasping, or abnormal eye movement that does not resolve with rest [B3-010].
corrections:
Cue "keep walking, slow it down" and stay beside the athlete pacing them.
Count the exhale out loud - "in two, out four" - until the athlete matches it unprompted.
Watch breathing against pace, not the clock, and slow the walk further if breathing hasn't settled.
If collapse, gasping, or abnormal eye findings appear, stop the drill immediately, treat as a medical emergency, and call for AED and emergency response without delay [B3-010].
transfer:
This is the same recovery breathing the athlete needs between rounds and after a hard exchange in sparring.
Bringing the body down from high arousal on command carries directly into managing stress outside the gym.

name: Post-Session Mobility
execution: Unloaded range work through the shoulders, hips and thoracic spine after the session.
what_good_looks_like:
Athlete carries each joint - shoulder, hip, thoracic spine - through its full range with no external load added.
Movement travels smooth and continuous, no pause-and-yank at the end position.
Breath stays steady and audible on every rep, matched to the movement's tempo.
Order runs shoulders, then hips, then thoracic spine, same sequence every session.

Bouncing or pulsing at the end of range instead of passing through it under control.
Breath held or ragged during the movement.

A band, partner, or added weight introduced into what should be bodyweight-only range work.
corrections:
Coach calls the breathing pace out loud - "in, out" - until the rhythm resets.
Coach places a hand at the end-range point and asks for a still hold there instead of a bounce.
Coach names the skipped joint out loud and sends the athlete back to that station before moving on.
Coach removes the added load or partner resistance and restarts the rep as bodyweight only.

name: Interval Work — Round Structure
execution: Work and rest intervals matched to the athlete's competition or training round structure. Interval length follows the applicable sanctioning body's round format for that age and class.
what_good_looks_like:
Round length and rest period match the athlete's sanctioned format exactly, one minute rest between rounds [A5-147][A6-022].
Output stays high through the closing seconds of the round, not just the opening minute.
Corner or timer calls "time" and the athlete stops output immediately and moves to the rest interval.
Activity-to-rest ratio holds steady across rounds instead of collapsing round to round [A5-004].
what_bad_looks_like:
Athlete front-loads round one and fades sharply by round two or three, output dropping late in each round [A5-004].
Rest interval runs long or short against the sanctioned one-minute standard [A5-147][A6-022].
Athlete paces to a generic clock instead of the round format for their actual age and class [A5-147][A6-022].
Movement and punch output stop several seconds before the bell instead of at the bell.
corrections:
Coach runs the actual round and rest length on a visible timer, no estimating by feel.
Coach calls out remaining time at fixed intervals so the athlete learns to hold pace to the bell.
Coach checks the athlete's age and class against the sanctioning body's format before setting the round length, not a generic interval [A5-147][A6-022].
Coach flags any late-round drop in output on the spot and has the athlete repeat the round at the same target pace.
transfer:
Holding output to the actual bell, not to a felt sense of time, is what separates a rehearsed pace from a fight pace.
Pacing across a full round instead of spending everything early carries directly into how the athlete manages effort in competition and in any task with a fixed time limit.

name: Continuous Aerobic Base
execution: Sustained low-intensity continuous work. Boxing bout energetics evidence is drawn from small adult male samples, so this is applied as general preparation rather than as a boxing-calibrated prescription.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing stays steady and controlled through the full duration, no gasping.
Pace holds constant from first minute to last - no early surge, no late fade.
Shoulders stay down, jaw loose, stride or footwork rhythm even throughout.
Athlete can speak in short phrases without gulping for air.

Breathing turns ragged and audible early in the session.
Stops or walks repeatedly instead of sustaining continuous movement.
Shoulders ride up toward the ears as fatigue sets in.

Call the pace out loud or set a metronome/pad rhythm and hold the group to it.
Walk alongside the athlete and cue "nose breathing, relax the jaw" until the pattern settles.
Drop the intensity a notch the moment gasping appears rather than letting them grind through it.
Shorten the work segment, rebuild the duration once the pace holds clean.

name: Skipping — Continuous
execution: Continuous skipping at a sustainable rhythm.
what_good_looks_like:
Rope turns from the wrists, not the shoulders.
Feet stay under the hips with a low, quiet bounce.
Landing is on the balls of the feet, heels lightly kissing down between skips.

Shoulders rolling the rope instead of the wrists.
Heels slamming flat on every landing.

Drop to a walk-in-place rhythm with no rope, rebuild timing, then reintroduce the rope.

name: Skipping — Varied

Staying light and unhurried under a surprise switch is the same poise needed when a fight plan stops working mid-round.

name: Bodyweight Lower Push

what_good_looks_like:
Feet flat, weight even across the whole foot through the entire rep.
Knees track in line with the toes on both the way down and the way up.
Hips and knees reach the same depth on every repetition, not just the first one.
Torso stays upright with a neutral spine, no forward collapse at the bottom.

Knees cave inward on the descent or the ascent.

Lower back rounds at the bottom of the squat.

name: Bodyweight Upper Push
execution: Press-up pattern with a scaled variation available for every athlete.
what_good_looks_like:
Straight line from shoulders through hips to ankles (or knees, in the scaled version) held for the entire rep.
Chest reaches the same depth every repetition before the press begins.
Elbows track at roughly a 45-degree angle from the torso, not flared out to the sides.
Full elbow lockout at the top, same down-up tempo rep after rep.
what_bad_looks_like:
Hips sag toward the floor or pike upward, breaking the straight line.
Head drops first and leads the movement instead of the chest.
Range of motion shortens - the chest stops short of a consistent depth.
Elbows flare out near 90 degrees and shoulders creep up toward the ears.
corrections:

purpose: Pulling strength to balance pushing volume

name: Hinge Pattern
execution: Hip hinge with a neutral spine, loaded only once the unloaded pattern is consistent.
what_good_looks_like:
Hips push back first, knees stay soft, spine holds one neutral line from head to tailbone.
Bar or hands track close along the thighs on the way down and up.
Shoulders and hips rise together on the drive up, no lag between them.
Athlete returns to full standing hip extension at the top, not a lean-back.
what_bad_looks_like:
Spine rounds or overextends in the lumbar region during the descent.
Knees drive forward and dominate the movement, turning the hinge into a squat.
Bar or hands drift away from the body, so the load path bows outward.
Hips shoot up first on the drive, shoulders lag behind.
corrections:
Cue "hips back into the wall behind you" and place an actual wall or bench there for feedback.
Have the athlete hold a dowel along their spine, three points of contact, to expose rounding immediately.
Drop the load and rebuild the pattern empty-handed until the bar path stays vertical and close.
Cue "push the floor away" on the drive to force hips and shoulders to rise on the same line.

The hinge is the base for the clinch, for picking an opponent's weight off balance, and for any lift or carry outside the gym.
A spine that holds its line under load here is the same spine that holds up under a shove, a takedown attempt, or a heavy bag in the arms.

purpose: Unilateral stability for stance and pivots

name: Rotational Medicine Ball Throw
execution: Rotational throw against a wall. Coach checks that the sequence starts at the ground rather than the arms.

Hips rotate before shoulders, and shoulders rotate before the arms - the ball leaves the hands last in the chain.
Rear foot pivots and drives into the floor as the throw begins, weight moving up through the legs before the torso turns.
Ball travels in a flat rotational arc into the wall, arms only extending at the very end of the motion.
Athlete resets into a loaded stance between reps, feet already placed for the next turn.
what_bad_looks_like:
Arms initiate the throw while the hips and legs stay passive.
Feet stay flat and square through the whole rep, no pivot on the rear foot.

Athlete bends forward at the waist to add force instead of turning off the ground.

Coach puts a hand on the athlete's hip and calls the pivot out loud so the ground-driven turn happens first, before the arms move.
Coach breaks the throw into separate ground-hip-shoulder-arm segments and has the athlete pause at each link before continuing, using the same phase vocabulary boxing technique is already broken down into for coaching cues [A6-055].
Coach stands behind the athlete and watches the rear foot on every rep, stopping the set if the heel stays planted.
Coach drops the ball weight until the correct order is visible, then rebuilds load once the sequence holds.

name: Countermovement Jump
execution: Maximal vertical jump. Also usable as a readiness measure when recorded consistently, though a boxing-specific threshold has not been established.
what_good_looks_like:
Rapid downward dip immediately reversed into an upward drive, no pause at the bottom.
Arms swing back through the dip and snap forward and up through takeoff.
Full extension of ankles, knees, and hips at the instant of takeoff.
Soft landing with knees bent, absorbing the impact without collapsing.
what_bad_looks_like:
Pause or hold at the bottom of the dip before driving upward.
Knees collapse inward on landing.
Arm swing disconnected from leg drive, firing early or lagging behind.
Jump height swings widely from session to session with no readable trend.
corrections:
Cue "load and go" and count the dip-to-drive tempo out loud to kill the pause.
Stand in front of the athlete to watch the knee line on landing and cue "knees over toes."
Drill the arm swing and the leg drive as separate reps, then reintegrate them on your count.
Lock the measurement device, surface, footwear, and time of day so session-to-session numbers are actually comparable.

name: Anti-Rotation Hold
execution: Hold against a lateral band pull without rotating. Trains the trunk to resist rather than produce rotation.
what_good_looks_like:
Feet stay planted, hips and shoulders stay square to the anchor point throughout the hold.
Band tension pulls the torso sideways and the torso does not follow it.
Breathing stays steady and rhythmic, no bracing-and-holding-breath pattern.
Hands and arms stay still relative to the trunk — the block moves as one piece.
what_bad_looks_like:
Shoulders open toward or away from the band pull.
Hips rotate before the shoulders do, so the trunk unwinds from the bottom up.
Athlete leans instead of resisting — trades rotation for lateral collapse.
Breath gets held, then dumped, causing the trunk to lose tension mid-hold.
corrections:
Reduce band tension or step closer to the anchor until square posture returns.
Cue "lock the belt buckle to the target" and physically tap the hip that drifts.
Slow the exposure — have the athlete step into tension rather than receive it suddenly.
Reset stance width and re-cue exhale-through-the-hold before resuming.
transfer:
This is the same trunk stiffness a boxer needs when eating a check hook or a body shot without getting spun off the centerline [A5-018].
Outside the gym it is the brace that keeps a lifter's spine still under an offset load.

purpose: Trunk and grip endurance under load

name: Seated Combination Work
target_behavior: Punch combinations from a seated base
purpose: Punch combinations from a seated base
execution: Combinations delivered from the athlete's seated base. Range and target height are set to the athlete rather than to a standard.
what_good_looks_like:
Hands return fully to guard after each strike, and the seat stays planted through contact.
The combination runs as one continuous sequence, strike into strike, with no pause between shots.
Wind-up, extension, and retraction are each visible as separate phases even from the seated base [A6-055].
Target height and reach match the athlete's own seated range rather than a standing measurement.

Athlete rises off the seat or leans the torso forward to manufacture extra reach.

name: Single-Arm Adaptation
target_behavior: Boxing patterns adapted to one working arm
purpose: Boxing patterns adapted to one working arm
execution: Technical patterns adapted for a single working arm, with guard and defensive responsibilities redistributed accordingly.
what_good_looks_like:
Lead arm holds guard and throws every strike; rear hand never leaves the temple or rib line.
Head and feet move on every exchange, creating angles the missing arm can no longer create [A8-004].
Combinations shorten to lead-hand variations thrown off footwork, not off a planted stance.
Chin stays tucked behind the lead shoulder through the full sequence, not just at the start.

Rear hand drops while the athlete moves, leaving the head exposed.
Shoulders square up to compensate for the missing arm, flattening the guard.

Feet stay planted, so the whole adaptation is asked of the arm instead of the body [A8-004][A3-021].

Stop the sequence, reset both hands to guard, restart from stance.
Touch the exposed temple or rib so the athlete feels the gap directly.
Cut the combination down to two punches until the guard holds through the whole exchange.

name: Sensory-Adapted Cue Drill
execution: Coach delivers cues through the athlete's available channel — visual, tactile, or verbal. Cue modality is agreed with the athlete beforehand.
what_good_looks_like:
Athlete responds within one beat of the cue, no visible search or hesitation.
Coach delivers the cue through the single pre-agreed channel only.

Coach stacks two or three channels into one delivery - visual, verbal, and tactile at once - instead of keeping instruction load low [A1-039].
Athlete freezes, looks to teammates, or delays response - the cue isn't landing on the agreed channel.

Reading a single clear cue under light contact is the same skill as reading an opponent's tell in live sparring.

Coach calls the rotation aloud and balances station numbers before the next round starts.
Coach demonstrates rope timing at half speed, then rebuilds it to full tempo with the participant.

Coach calls interval start and stop audibly and moves the group on that cue, not on individual pace.

Feet reset to stance after every combination, no flat-footed throws.
Guard hand returns to cheek before the next strike starts.
